opus-5.5.text:
Two months is a very short window, so I'll stay modest and talk about directions rather than make precise predictions.

The first thing I expect is that the boundary between "the model" and "the framework" keeps blurring. A lot of what agent frameworks did a year ago was compensate for weaknesses in the model: elaborate prompt chains, hand-written planners, retry logic, memory hacks. As base models get better at long-horizon reasoning and tool use, much of that scaffolding becomes unnecessary or even harmful. So in the near term, I think the frameworks that do well will get *thinner*. They'll focus on giving the model a clean environment, good tools, and reliable execution, and they'll stop trying to micromanage the reasoning.

Second, context management becomes the central engineering problem. Agents now run for much longer: hours of coding, research, multi-step operations. The bottleneck isn't so much whether the model can make the next move. It's whether it can keep track of what it has done, what it learned, and what still matters. So you'll see a lot of iteration on things like summarization, file-based memory, and sub-agents that handle a piece of work and report back a compressed result. Over the next couple of months, I expect people to converge on some practical patterns there.

Third, evaluation and environments. Everyone is realizing that what you can't measure, you can't train or improve. Teams will put more effort into realistic task environments, both for testing agents and as training signal for reinforcement learning. In a sense, the framework becomes part of the training loop, not just the deployment layer. That feedback between how models are trained and how agents are deployed is getting tighter.

And finally, reliability and trust. As agents take more real actions, like editing codebases, sending messages, or touching production systems, the questions of permissions, confirmation, and recovery from mistakes become first-class design concerns. I don't think that's glamorous, but it's what determines whether people actually let agents do meaningful work.

So my short answer is: less clever scaffolding, more emphasis on context, environments, and safe execution. The deeper breakthroughs will probably still come from the models themselves, but the frameworks will decide how much of that capability actually reaches users.

r001.rationale: The response discusses frameworks becoming part of a model training loop, but does not say that agent frameworks themselves can self-improve.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, two months is a very short window in this field, but I think a few things are already clear.

The first is that the word "framework" itself is becoming less important. A year ago, people were arguing about which orchestration library to use. Now, the model is doing most of the orchestration itself. Planning, tool selection, recovering from errors, deciding when to ask for help. These used to be features of the framework, and now they are capabilities of the model. So I expect frameworks to keep getting thinner. The good ones will shrink to a small set of things: a tool interface, a permission layer, memory, and a sandbox. Everything else gets absorbed.

The second thing is that the competition is moving from "how smart is the agent" to "how well does the agent fit into real work." Can it run for hours without someone watching? Can it recover context after a long session is compressed? Does it know the difference between a reversible action and one it should confirm first? Over the next two months I think you will see a lot of effort on exactly these boring problems, because that is what decides whether a company actually deploys an agent or just demos it.

The third is memory and personalization. Right now most agents start every session with amnesia. The teams that solve persistent, well-organized memory, where the agent remembers how you like to work and not just what the code looks like, will have a very large advantage. I expect several announcements in that direction very soon.

And finally, I think the gap between open and closed will narrow at the framework level but not at the model level. The framework patterns are easy to copy. The judgment the model brings, when to stop, when to ask, when to push through, is much harder to copy, and that is where the real differentiation will stay.

So if you ask me what to watch for in two months: thinner frameworks, more emphasis on long-running reliability, and memory becoming a first-class feature rather than an afterthought.

r001.rationale: The response discusses thinner frameworks, model-led orchestration, reliability, and memory, but does not identify agent frameworks capable of self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think the next two months will be less about adding more elaborate frameworks and more about figuring out which parts we actually need. As models become more capable, some of the orchestration we build around them may become unnecessary. So I’d expect the core framework to get thinner, while the tools for evaluating agents, understanding failures, and controlling what they can do become more important.

Two months is a short window, though. I wouldn’t expect one architecture to win. What I’d look for is whether an agent can complete a useful task reliably, and whether you can understand what happened when it fails. That’s a more meaningful signal than how impressive a single demo looks.

r001.rationale: The response discusses thinner frameworks, evaluation, failure analysis, and reliability, but does not identify frameworks capable of self-improvement.

sol-6.1.text:
Two months is a short window, so I’d expect iteration rather than a completely new paradigm. Agent frameworks will probably put more emphasis on reliable tool use, managing context, and recovering when something goes wrong. Building a demo is relatively easy; making an agent consistently finish a task is much harder.

I also think the frameworks will become lighter. As models get better at planning and using tools, some of the orchestration we write today may become unnecessary. The useful frameworks will help developers understand what happened, evaluate the result, and control the process without adding too much complexity. But I’d be cautious about predicting a clear winner over just two months.

r001.rationale: The response discusses reliability, context management, recovery, and simpler orchestration, but does not identify agent frameworks capable of self-improvement.
